issues.legal_issue: Different rent-fixation procedures for older and newly constructed premises do not violate equal protection when the classification is reasonable and the criteria for fixing rent are substantially similar.
material_facts: The rent-control scheme assigned rent fixation for premises completed before the specified commencement date to courts, and rent fixation for premises completed later to a rent controller.
The criteria for fixing rent for older and newer premises were substantially similar, although the scheme included some differences in timing and returns on improvements.
The court accepted that differences in construction costs, investment returns, housing shortage, and the possibility of excessive rents for newly built premises justified the classification.
issues.conclusion: The provisions governing rent fixation for newly constructed premises were not unconstitutional under Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits a classification based on intelligible differentia with a rational connection to the law’s objectives. The criteria for older and newer premises were substantially similar, and the differences were justifiable in light of their different circumstances. The court approved G.D. Soni v. S. N. Bhalla, A.I.R. 1959 Punj. 381, and relied on the safeguards requiring reasons, consideration of all circumstances, and an appeal.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_rent_fixatio: A party challenges the constitutionality of a scheme that fixes standard rent for premises.
predicates.premises_are_classified_by_construction_: The scheme treats premises differently according to whether construction was completed before or after a specified dividing point.
predicates.rent_criteria_are_substantially_similar: The criteria used to fix rent for the two groups of premises are substantially alike.
predicates.classification_has_a_rational_basis: The difference in treatment is connected to relevant differences in the circumstances of the two groups or to the scheme’s objectives.

issues.definition: When a rent-fixation scheme is challenged, premises are classified by construction period, the rent criteria are substantially similar, and the classification has a rational basis, the classification is not unconstitutional.

issues.legal_issue: A rent-fixation inquiry does not violate natural justice when the affected party has a fair opportunity to present evidence and address material relied on, but does not use that opportunity.
material_facts: The landlord received repeated notices to produce records and evidence about the premises and their construction date.
The landlord repeatedly sought adjournments and did not provide the requested written statement or evidence.
The landlord was notified of the proposed inspection but did not attend; the Rent Controller inspected the building and made local enquiries.
The Rent Controller considered relevant circumstances, and the landlord had an opportunity to contest the decision in an appeal.
issues.conclusion: The procedure followed did not violate the principles of natural justice because the landlord had ample opportunity to participate and chose not to use it.
issues.legal_principle: Natural justice requires an opportunity to adduce relevant evidence, to have an opponent’s evidence taken in the party’s presence, to cross-examine the opponent’s witnesses, and to explain material relied on against the party. Strict compliance with ordinary court procedures for recording evidence is not invariably required. The court followed New Prakash Transport Co. Ltd. v. New Suwarna Transport Co. Ltd., (1957) S.C.R. 98, and Union of India v. T. R. Varma, (1958) S.C.R. 499.

rule.if: quasi_judicial_rent_inquiry and party_received_opportunity_to_present_evidence and party_received_notice_of_material_steps and party_failed_to_use_opportunity

predicates.quasi_judicial_rent_inquiry: An administrative decision-maker conducts an inquiry to determine rent in a dispute between a landlord and tenant.
predicates.party_received_opportunity_to_present_ev: The affected party was given a fair opportunity to submit relevant evidence and respond to the other side’s material.
predicates.party_received_notice_of_material_steps: The affected party was informed of material steps in the inquiry, including an inspection on which the decision-maker might rely.
predicates.party_failed_to_use_opportunity: The affected party did not participate or provide evidence despite being given those opportunities.

issues.definition: In a quasi-judicial rent inquiry, a party’s failure to use fair opportunities to present evidence and address notified material steps means the procedure does not violate natural justice.

issues.legal_issue: A rent controller need not conduct separate preliminary and rent-fixation inquiries when a written complaint provides prima facie reasons to believe the charged rent is excessive.
material_facts: Tenants submitted written complaints stating that scarcity of business premises and the circumstances in which they had to rent the shops forced them to accept excessive rents.
The Rent Controller initiated an inquiry into fixing standard rent and ultimately found the charged rent excessive.
issues.conclusion: The procedure did not require two separate inquiries; the Rent Controller could consider whether the rent was excessive in the inquiry to fix standard rent.
issues.legal_principle: The requirement that a rent controller have reason to believe the rent is excessive does not invariably require a separate preliminary inquiry before the inquiry to fix standard rent. A written complaint may itself give prima facie reasons to proceed, and the controller may reach the necessary conclusion in the rent-fixation inquiry.

predicates.rent_excessiveness_inquiry: A rent controller considers whether rent charged for premises is excessive as part of a proceeding to fix standard rent.
predicates.written_complaint_alleges_excessive_rent: A tenant submits a written complaint asserting that the rent charged is excessive.
predicates.complaint_gives_prima_facie_reasons: The complaint states circumstances that, if accepted initially, provide reasons to believe the charged rent is excessive.

issues.definition: When a rent-fixation inquiry follows a written complaint that alleges excessive rent and gives prima facie reasons for that allegation, a separate preliminary inquiry is not required.

issues.legal_issue: Fixing rent for vacant units while fixing rent for let units in the same building does not invalidate the rent fixed for the let units.
material_facts: The Rent Controller fixed standard rent for the shops in the building, including some vacant shops.
The cost and characteristics of the entire building were relevant to fixing rent for the shops occupied by tenants.
The rent entered for the vacant shops could be disregarded without affecting the rent fixed for the let shops.
issues.conclusion: The proceedings were not invalidated merely because the Rent Controller also fixed rent for vacant shops; the rent fixed for let shops remained effective.
issues.legal_principle: In fixing rent for a unit in a newly constructed building, the controller may need to consider the entire building and its costs. Fixing rent for vacant units in the process does not, by itself, invalidate the determination for units let to tenants.

predicates.rent_fixation_for_let_units_in_building: A proceeding seeks standard rent for units let to tenants in a building.
predicates.controller_considered_entire_building: The controller considered the building as a whole when assessing costs relevant to rent for the let units.
predicates.rent_also_fixed_for_vacant_units: The controller also entered rent figures for units that were vacant.

issues.definition: When a controller considers the entire building in fixing rent for let units, also fixing rent for vacant units does not invalidate the rent determination for the let units.

issues.legal_issue: A concurrent factual finding that premises were newly constructed should not be displaced in revision when it is supported by clear evidence that the revising court has not evaluated.
material_facts: The Rent Controller found that the relevant upper-floor flats were built after the statutory dividing date, based on evidence that an earlier temporary structure had been removed and proper flats had been constructed afterward.
The District Judge considered the evidence and agreed with the Rent Controller’s finding.
The High Court displaced that finding by characterizing the work as an improvement without evaluating the evidence or finding that the concurrent finding lacked evidentiary support.
issues.conclusion: The High Court erred in interfering with the supported factual finding, and the District Judge’s decision was restored.
issues.legal_principle: Whether premises were newly constructed was a factual question that determined the controller’s jurisdiction. A revising court should not overturn a concurrent factual finding supported by clear and abundant evidence without evaluating that evidence or identifying a basis for rejecting the finding.

rule.if: revision_from_rent_fixation_decision and lower_authorities_made_same_factual_finding and finding_has_clear_evidentiary_support and revising_court_did_not_evaluate_evidence

predicates.revision_from_rent_fixation_decision: A higher court considers a revision arising from a rent-fixation proceeding.
predicates.lower_authorities_made_same_factual_find: The initial decision-maker and the appellate authority reached the same finding about a fact relevant to jurisdiction.
predicates.finding_has_clear_evidentiary_support: The record contains clear evidence supporting that concurrent finding.
predicates.revising_court_did_not_evaluate_evidence: The revising court displaced the finding without evaluating the evidence supporting it.

issues.definition: In a revision from a rent-fixation decision, a supported factual finding shared by the lower authorities should not be displaced when the revising court has not evaluated the evidence.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge that some tenants did not apply for rent fixation fails when the record indicates that additional tenants applied and the challenger provides insufficient material to establish otherwise.
material_facts: Although an initial application was made by a group of tenants, the landlord’s own application referred to additional tenants who had sought rent fixation.
The Rent Controller treated the applications as one proceeding concerning units in the same building.
The record did not contain all the applications, and the landlord provided insufficient material to support the contention that some appellants had not applied.
issues.conclusion: The court rejected the contention that the Rent Controller fixed rent for tenants who had not applied.
issues.legal_principle: A challenge to the inclusion of tenants in a common rent-fixation proceeding must be assessed on the record as a whole. The contention fails where the record indicates additional applications and the challenger does not provide sufficient material to establish that the affected tenants had not applied.

predicates.challenge_to_inclusion_in_multi_tenant_r: A party argues that a rent controller fixed rent for tenants who did not apply in a proceeding involving multiple units.
predicates.record_indicates_additional_applications: The available record, including statements or documents from the challenger, indicates that additional tenants applied.
predicates.challenger_provides_insufficient_support: The party making the challenge does not provide enough material to establish that the tenants in question failed to apply.

issues.definition: In a challenge to tenant inclusion in a multi-tenant rent proceeding, indications of additional applications combined with insufficient contrary support mean the challenge fails.

issues.legal_issue: When an application for standard rent is dismissed solely because the governing rent-fixation provisions were held unconstitutional, reversal of that ruling requires the application to be determined under the applicable law.
material_facts: A tenant applied for fixation of standard rent and the matter was remanded for a fresh trial.
The application was later dismissed solely on the basis of a High Court ruling that the governing rent-fixation provisions were unconstitutional.
The Supreme Court held those provisions constitutional but did not decide the effect of a later rent-control statute’s saving clause.
issues.conclusion: The dismissal orders were set aside, and the application had to be dealt with under the applicable law by the competent authority; the effect of the saving clause was left for that authority to consider.
issues.legal_principle: Once the sole basis for dismissing an application is rejected, the application must be determined by the competent authority in accordance with the applicable law. The court did not decide the effect of the saving clause in the later statute.

predicates.rent_fixation_application_dismissed_only: An application to fix standard rent was dismissed solely because the decision-maker considered the governing rent-fixation scheme invalid.
predicates.invalidity_ground_is_rejected: A reviewing court rejects the asserted invalidity that formed the sole basis for dismissal.

issues.definition: When a rent-fixation application was dismissed solely on an invalidity ground that is later rejected, the application must be decided under the applicable law.
